title: Odisha Pattachitra
region: Odisha, especially Puri and surrounding areas
intro: Painted stories built from prepared surfaces, fine brush lines and richly worked borders.
tradition: Odisha Pattachitra includes paintings on prepared cloth as well as work on other surfaces and objects. The Government of Odisha describes religious, mythological and folk subjects, including stories associated with Jagannath and Krishna. There are other traditions also called Pattachitra; this page focuses on Odisha, not all regional practices. The Odisha Crafts Museum describes paintings in a range of media and notes contemporary as well as mythological subjects. An individual work is the creation of its maker: this tradition contains many hands and approaches.

Odisha Crafts Museum documents work in multiple media and a movement from traditional organic colours to modern substitutes, and from mythological to contemporary subjects. Materials and themes differ by maker.
process: The Odisha government describes one traditional method of preparing a cloth support with chalk and glue made from tamarind seeds. In that account, the border comes first, followed by a brush sketch, flat colours and fine finishing lines. Materials and order vary between makers and works. Its account describes colour sources including lampblack, mineral pigments and white made from shells. Contemporary practice can also use newer materials; do not assume a particular object uses natural pigments unless its own record says so.

title: Mithila / Madhubani painting
region: Mithila, including parts of Bihar and Nepal
intro: Paintings shaped by the people, occasions and stories of the Mithila region.
tradition: Mithila painting, often called Madhubani painting, is associated with the Mithila region of Bihar and adjoining parts of Nepal. Traditions do not stop at present-day national or state borders. India's handicrafts compendium describes paintings made on walls and floors and, today, on cloth, paper and canvas. Paintings have been made for occasions including weddings and festivals. Artists work with different visual languages: the compendium names kachni, bharni and godhana among them, while individual makers and communities can have their own distinctive approaches.
Mithila painting continues on paper, cloth and canvas as well as walls and floors. Artists draw on inherited practices and their own experiences; neither subject matter nor method is uniform.
process: Fine linework and filled fields of colour are among the approaches described in the handicrafts compendium. Their meaning and materials depend on the artist and the object; one work's palette should not be treated as a rule for the entire tradition. A painting may refer to ritual, the natural world, epics or an artist's own life. Look closely at who made it and what they say it represents before assigning a fixed meaning to a motif.

maker.name: Ganga Devi
maker.description: Mithila artist Ganga Devi is associated with kachni linework and paintings that include traditional subjects alongside personal experiences. Smarthistory discusses the range of her work and the tradition's social context.

title: Gond painting
intro: Artists draw on stories, memories and visual practices in many individual ways.
tradition: Gond is a broad community designation, and Gond painting is not a single uniform visual style. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) records work by many named artists, including Durga Bai, whose paintings draw on Gond Pardhan stories and folktales. The histories of household painting and contemporary work on portable surfaces overlap, but individual artists make their own choices. An account of one painter should not be treated as a complete account of everyone who works in the tradition.

Contemporary artists make distinct works informed by their experiences and training. IGNCA profiles many named painters; their individual accounts provide a starting point for learning about their work.
process: IGNCA records that Durga Bai learned digna, designs made on walls and floors for weddings and festivals, alongside her mother. Its profile connects her work with Burbaspur in Madhya Pradesh and with the stories she heard from her grandmother. Detail can carry a story as well as fill a surface. Instead of assuming each mark has a single shared meaning, read the artist's own description when one is available.

maker.name: Durga Bai Vyam
maker.description: Durga Bai Vyam is an artist whose work includes folktales and images rooted in her Gond Pardhan community. IGNCA describes the role of family, childhood painting and storytelling in her practice.

title: Warli painting
region: Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
intro: Human figures, animals and settings bring communities and their stories into view.
tradition: Warli painting is associated with Warli communities in western India, including parts of Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu. Regions overlap, and the practice cannot be reduced to a single administrative border. Paintings can depict gatherings and aspects of daily life. Individual makers and works are varied: avoid assuming every image depicts the same event or was made for the same purpose.
Contemporary practitioners work on a range of surfaces. Museum collections hold individual works by artists such as Jivya Soma Mashe, alongside the continuing practice of wall painting.
process: One traditional process described by craft sources uses a prepared wall and white rice-paste marks. Contemporary artists may use other materials, including paper, canvas and acrylic paint. The relationship between the ground, white marks and the surrounding space can make images feel rhythmic and active. That observation is a way to look, not a universal meaning assigned to every shape.

title: Kalamkari
region: Andhra Pradesh and other parts of India
intro: Kalamkari brings drawing, dyeing and cloth together. The name refers to pen work, while the label encompasses more than one local textile practice.
tradition: Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam are two important centres in Andhra Pradesh. Their practices differ: artists in Srikalahasti work with a pen, while hand-block printing is associated with Machilipatnam. Other historical textiles described as kalamkari come from elsewhere in India.

Kalamkari continues through individual workshops and new subjects. Practitioners adapt the craft for clothing, wall pieces and contemporary stories; neither all materials nor all designs follow one fixed historical recipe.
process: In hand-drawn practice, a maker applies designs with a bamboo pen. Dyeing can involve several stages and careful preparation of cloth; approaches and colours vary by maker. Some painted cottons use a mordant, which helps a dye attach to the fabric, and resist treatments that prevent colour reaching selected areas.

maker.name: Theertham Balaji
maker.description: In a 2010 interview, Srikalahasti artist Theertham Balaji described training under S. Rambhoji Naik, working mainly in natural dyes on cotton, and painting village life as well as religious subjects.

title: Dhokra
region: Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and other regions
intro: Dhokra, also spelled Dokra, is a family of metal-casting practices in which artisans use wax and clay to shape the final object.
tradition: Dhokra practices are documented in Odisha, West Bengal and Chhattisgarh, among other places. Objects and practices vary across communities and workshops. Dhokra can include figures, ornaments, boxes and other objects.
Artisans continue to make both functional and decorative work for changing uses and audiences. A name such as Dhokra describes related practices, not a single style or community.
process: In one documented lost-wax process, the maker shapes a clay core and builds the design with wax, often in fine threads. Clay layers surround it to make a mould. Heat melts the wax; molten metal fills the space it leaves. After cooling, the outer mould is broken and the casting is finished by hand.

title: Longpi pottery
intro: Longpi, or Nungbi, black pottery is associated with Tangkhul Naga makers in Manipur. Documented practices include shaping vessels by hand without a potter’s wheel.
tradition: Longpi is a living craft associated with villages in Ukhrul district. Its black-finished vessels include pieces for everyday and ceremonial use. Individual makers adapt shapes and techniques to their materials and customers.
Alongside cooking vessels, makers produce cups, kettles and other forms. The Indian Ministry of Tribal Affairs describes the tradition as an expression of Tangkhul knowledge and cultural identity.
process: In the process documented by NIFT for one artisan, powdered black serpentine stone is mixed with brown clay, shaped and beaten by hand, dried, polished and fired. The exact proportions and sequence can vary; the National Institute of Fashion Technology describes one maker’s practice rather than a rule for all potters.

title: Ajrakh block printing
intro: Layered block printing and resist dyeing build up colour on cloth.
tradition: Ajrakh is a family of block-printed textile practices associated with Kutch in Gujarat and with Sindh across the present-day India–Pakistan border. Asia InCH documents cloth made for garments and household use in Kutch. This entry begins there; it cannot describe every regional practice.
Makers and workshops make different choices about colour, pattern, scale and materials. A textile is the result of their decisions, not simply a catalogue of motifs.
process: The Kutch account describes printing with carved wooden blocks alongside repeated dyeing and resist processes. Indigo and madder are among the colour sources recorded; a particular textile may use different dyes. Alignment, washing and successive applications are part of the work.
materials: Cotton, carved blocks, dyes and resists

title: Kantha embroidery
intro: Running stitches hold layers of cloth together and create images, borders and texture.
tradition: Kantha describes several embroidered textiles associated with Bengal, including present-day West Bengal and Bangladesh. Asia InCH describes West Bengal examples made from layers of worn saris and dhotis, often stitched by women.
Some examples are quilts, while others serve as covers, wraps or contemporary textiles. Their images and stitches reflect individual makers and their circumstances.
process: In one documented method, layers of cloth are held together with running stitches, sometimes using thread drawn from old sari borders. Layers, colours and stitches vary by maker and by object.
materials: Reused cloth, thread and running stitches

title: Bidriware
intro: Darkened metal surfaces are inlaid with contrasting designs.
tradition: Bidriware takes its name from Bidar in Karnataka. It includes vessels and other objects made with an alloy and contrasting inlay. Its history and present-day forms span changing patrons, uses and workshops.
Craft accounts describe the surface finishing and inlay work; look at a particular maker and object for the materials actually used.
process: A documented process casts an alloy, engraves a design, and sets wire or sheet in the cut grooves. A finishing treatment darkens the body while the inlaid metal remains bright. The method and alloys can vary.

title: Phad painting
region: Bhilwara and other parts of Rajasthan
intro: Painted scrolls carry stories that are performed and retold.
tradition: IGNCA describes Phad as painted scrolls associated with Rajasthan, made by artists of the Joshi lineage and used by Bhopa performers who narrate the stories depicted. Accounts include scrolls devoted to local deities and legendary heroes.
The scroll is part of a relationship between painters, performers and audiences. Contemporary works can take different forms and scales; this page does not treat every scroll as identical.
process: Paintings place many episodes on a cloth scroll. IGNCA describes an example displayed on a bamboo frame during narration; the scroll can be folded for travel. Refer to an individual work for its materials and dimensions.

title: Molela terracotta
intro: Clay plaques and figures made for devotion, homes and new settings.
tradition: The craft associated with Molela in Rajasthan includes modelled terracotta plaques with figures and other forms. The Government of India’s geographical-indications compendium records the craft and its location.
Makers work for different communities and contexts; a plaque’s identity and purpose should be read from its own maker or record.
process: Clay is shaped into relief forms and fired. The government compendium describes making and firing as part of the craft. Finishing and colour differ between examples.

title: Kalighat painting
intro: Bold lines and painted figures from a changing urban tradition.
tradition: The Victoria and Albert Museum traces Kalighat painting to nineteenth-century Kolkata, where patua painters made works for a broad market. Their subjects developed from deities and mythological figures to include other aspects of urban life.
The Metropolitan Museum notes that descendants of painters continue working in the Kalighat area. Individual works and artists should be encountered on their own terms.
process: The V&A describes painters using bold outlines and colours on paper. The Met’s records document watercolor and other materials in particular works; these should not be assumed for every painting.

title: Channapatna lacquer toys
intro: Turned wooden forms are shaped and finished with colour.
tradition: Channapatna in Karnataka is associated with lacquered wooden toys and objects. Government and craft accounts describe the making tradition and the workshops involved.
Toys and contemporary objects take different shapes and uses; the name refers to a place and a field of practice rather than one unchanging design.
process: The craft accounts describe wood shaped on a lathe and finished with lacquer. Materials and colour treatments differ, so check the source for each object.

title: Kutch embroidery
intro: Many communities and individual makers create distinct embroidered textiles.
tradition: Embroidery in Kutch is not one style. The Craft Revival Trust documents different regional practices, including embroidery associated with Meghwal makers in the Banni region. Communities, stitches and uses differ.
Avoid assigning a community, a maker or a symbolic meaning to a textile solely from its appearance. The history of a particular piece is best learned from the maker and its documented record.
process: Needlework builds patterns on a cloth or other ground. Different Kutch practices use different stitches, materials and layouts; not every embroidered object includes mirrors.

title: Monpa handmade paper
region: Tawang and West Kameng, Arunachal Pradesh
intro: Sheets made by hand from plant fibre for writing, printing and other uses.
tradition: Monpa handmade paper is associated with Tawang and West Kameng in Arunachal Pradesh. An Indian government account describes an effort to support the craft in Tawang; the local tourism account calls the paper Mon-Shug.
Paper is both a craft and a support for other visual and written work. Its uses and the makers who produce it deserve attention alongside the finished sheet.
process: The National Institute of Design describes gathering the shrub’s inner bark, boiling and beating it into pulp, and pouring the diluted mixture into frames to dry as sheets. Its 2026 invitation project shaped the handmade paper into a Mithun silhouette.

title: Majuli mask making
intro: Expressive masks shaped, painted and used in the cultural life of Majuli.
tradition: The district administration describes mask making at Samaguri Satra on Majuli, Assam. The masks are connected to the visual world of Bhaona, while this entry focuses on their making as objects.
Individual makers and workshops make different characters, sizes and expressions. These crafted forms belong to a living practice rather than a single fixed design.
process: Assam’s industries department describes masks made from materials including bamboo, cloth, clay and wood, then painted. Not every mask uses the same combination of materials.
materials: Bamboo, cloth, clay, wood and paint

title: Kaavi wall art
intro: Red and white wall surfaces are worked to reveal a design.
tradition: Kaavi is a wall-art practice associated with Goa and the wider Konkan coast. A Museum of Christian Art account describes Kaavi as a sgraffito technique using lime plaster and natural pigments.
Examples appear in different architectural and religious settings. Buildings and communities have distinct histories, so a motif should be understood in its own setting.
process: The museum describes a red-and-white process in which a coloured layer and lime ground are worked to create an image. Particular materials and conservation methods differ between sites.
materials: Lime plaster and red pigment on walls

sources.label: Goa Department of Information: Kaavi art

title: Panipat durries
intro: Flat-woven floor coverings from a city with a long textile industry.
tradition: Panipat is a centre for rugs and other handloom textiles in Haryana. An application in India’s geographical indications register and an Asia InCH craft account identify the city with durries and floor coverings.

A field study follows a panja durrie from hand production toward the wider textile market. Asia InCH also describes geometric floor coverings associated with Haryana. Individual floor coverings have different makers, uses and designs.
process: A study of Panipat production describes weavers inserting coloured weft yarns on small or medium frames, and the later use of handlooms. Fibre, loom, pattern and the balance of hand and industrial work vary by workshop.
materials: Woven yarn and textile floor coverings

title: Chamba rumal embroidery
intro: Images embroidered on cloth, often worked from both sides.
tradition: The Chamba rumal is a pictorial embroidery associated with Chamba in Himachal Pradesh. Government and craft accounts document embroidered covers and other textiles in different sizes.
Designs and subjects vary; the hands that draw, stitch and commission a rumal all contribute to the history of a particular work.
process: One documented stitch is do-rukha, a double satin stitch worked so the embroidery can be read from both faces of the cloth. Other stitches and approaches are also used.

title: Sohrai and Khovar painting
intro: Distinct wall-painting practices carried by artists and communities in Hazaribagh.
tradition: Jharkhand’s Tribal Welfare Research Institute documents Sohrai and Khovar as two wall-painting practices associated with Hazaribagh. They are related in place but should not be treated as identical.

Asia InCH associates Sohrai painting with the harvest season and distinguishes it from Khovar, which is associated with weddings. Individual women artists and communities bring their own knowledge to the work.
process: Asia InCH describes natural pigments and prepared wall surfaces, with tools including twig or leaf brushes and combs that create texture. Materials and methods vary between makers and works.

title: Aranmula metal mirrors
intro: A reflective surface made by casting and polishing metal rather than silvering glass.
tradition: Aranmula Kannadi are handcrafted metal mirrors associated with Aranmula in Kerala. Kerala Tourism describes the work of specialist artisan households and distinguishes these mirrors from ordinary glass mirrors.
Unlike a glass mirror, the reflective surface is polished metal. An Asia InCH account describes a copper-and-tin alloy; its exact composition and working knowledge belong to the makers.
process: Kerala Tourism describes metal casting followed by careful polishing to create a reflective front surface. Frames and proportions differ across examples.

title: Ryndia weaving
region: Ri Bhoi and other areas, Meghalaya
intro: Eri silk is spun, dyed and woven into textiles in Meghalaya.
tradition: Meghalaya Tourism describes Ryndia as an eri-silk textile practice sustained by weavers and other workers, especially women. The region’s wider textile practices include distinct Khasi, Garo and Jaintia work.

In a 2015 V&A account, weaver Kwickstar Tmung describes learning natural dyeing and weaving from her mother and teaching others. Eri work is connected to family knowledge and livelihoods as well as finished cloth.
process: The V&A describes rearing eri silkworms, spinning the fibre, dyeing yarn and weaving it on floor or frame looms in Meghalaya. A documented chaddar in this atlas was handspun and handwoven; materials and processes vary across textiles.
materials: Eri silk yarn and woven cloth

title: Mizo Puanchei
intro: A woven textile with bands and supplementary-yarn designs.
tradition: Mizo Puanchei is a woven textile from Mizoram. The state’s Art and Culture Department describes its importance as clothing and the skill needed to make its elaborate designs.
Textiles are made and worn in changing contexts, from family use to contemporary markets. Specific patterns and meanings belong to their makers and communities.
process: The state account describes a traditional loin loom, supplementary yarns used to create designs, and multiple woven pieces joined to form a complete puan. Yarn choices have changed over time.

title: Naga textile weaving
intro: Distinct woven cloths made by different Naga communities.
tradition: Naga textiles are a diverse group of weaving practices, not one pattern. IGNCA describes different cloths, techniques and associations among communities in Nagaland.
The National Crafts Museum documents individual shawls with their own histories. A design seen on one textile should not be attributed to all Naga communities.
process: IGNCA describes tension-loom weaving and a range of bands, stripes and other arrangements. Yarn, design and use vary with the weaver, community and garment.

title: Phulkari embroidery
intro: Embroidered cloth made with patterned stitches across the Punjab region.
tradition: Phulkari is an embroidery associated with the Punjab region and with communities in present-day Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan. The government craft compendium records this geographic reach.
The textiles are made and exchanged in different family and social settings. Colours, patterns and names vary by maker and community, including across today’s national borders.
process: The Philadelphia Museum of Art describes darning stitch as a principal technique in Phulkari and documents silk embroidery on handwoven cotton khaddar. Stitch choices, colours and the amount of visible ground differ among textiles.

title: Lepcha weaving
intro: Narrow woven bands of colour, joined and used in clothing and other textiles.
tradition: Lepcha weaving is associated with the Lepcha community in Sikkim and adjoining Himalayan areas. The National Institute of Design and Asia InCH describe Lepcha woven textiles and the materials used.
Designs, materials and uses are part of living community knowledge. The woven objects made by individual people have histories beyond a single regional label.
process: Asia InCH describes work on a backstrap loom, with narrow woven widths sometimes joined together. Cotton and wool are among materials recorded today; older accounts also describe plant fibres.
materials: Cotton or wool yarn and woven cloth

title: Thanjavur painting
intro: Painted images with raised decoration and luminous foil.
tradition: Thanjavur painting takes its name from Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu. India’s National Museum describes works with vivid colour, gold foil and raised gesso decoration.
The museum holds individual paintings that can be studied for their subjects, materials and histories. Artists continue to make and adapt the form.
process: A Craft Revival Trust collection account describes the use of gesso and gold in a particular Tanjore painting. The materials and technique of a given work should be checked against its own record.
materials: Paint, gesso and gold foil on prepared supports

sources.label: National Museum: Thanjavur paintings

title: Cheriyal scroll painting
intro: Narrative images painted on cloth in a Nakashi painting tradition.
tradition: Cheriyal scroll painting is associated with Telangana and Nakashi painters. Government and craft accounts describe painted narratives and the relationships between painters, storytellers and audiences.
Artists also make works at different scales for contemporary settings. One scroll or one family’s practice cannot represent every maker.
process: Asia InCH describes cotton cloth prepared as a painting surface and used for narrative compositions. Materials and preparation vary by artist.

sources.label: Incredible India: Cheriyal paintings

title: Tripura Risa textile
intro: A handwoven cloth with varied uses and community significance.
tradition: The Government of India describes Risa as a handwoven textile rooted in Tripuri community traditions. It documents weaving by women and household-based production in the state.
Risa can be worn or presented in different ways. Patterns and meanings vary across makers and communities; no single piece captures the whole tradition.
process: The government account describes weaving on loin or backstrap looms. Fibres, designs and finishing depend on the weaver and the individual textile.

title: Khurja pottery
intro: Glazed ceramic forms from a major pottery-making centre.
tradition: Khurja in Uttar Pradesh is a centre for pottery and glazed ceramics. India’s geographic-indications register identifies Khurja Pottery, and craft accounts describe its workshops and products.
Cups, vessels and decorative forms are made in different ways and at different scales. Maker and production details should be checked for each object.
process: Asia InCH describes Khurja’s glazed pottery practice. Forming, glazing and firing vary by workshop, material and piece.
materials: Clay, ceramic glazes and kiln firing

title: Aipan painting
intro: Painted designs made for domestic and ceremonial settings.
tradition: Aipan is a visual art associated with Kumaon in Uttarakhand. The Pithoragarh district administration describes designs made on walls, paper and cloth.
Aipan has connections to household and ceremonial occasions, while artists also explore it in other settings. The design of an individual work should be read in its own context.
process: Asia InCH describes freehand designs made with rice paste and geru, a red clay, among other materials. Artists make different patterns for different settings and occasions.
materials: Rice paste, prepared grounds, walls and other surfaces

title: Nicobari mat weaving
region: Nicobar Islands, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
intro: Pandanus leaves are prepared and woven into mats.
tradition: Asia InCH identifies chatrai or hileuoi as a mat associated with Nicobari people of the Nicobar Islands. It is a useful floor covering as well as an example of skilled fibre work.
The Nicobar Islands are home to diverse people and knowledge. A mat’s maker, community and use should be identified from the record of that particular object.
process: The craft account describes selecting, drying, trimming and splitting pandanus leaves before they are woven. The resulting pattern and finish vary.

title: Nek Chand’s Rock Garden
intro: A sculptural environment made with recovered materials.
tradition: The Chandigarh district administration identifies Nek Chand as the founder of the Rock Garden, a sculpture garden in Chandigarh. Its figures and environments are a particular artist’s work, not a claim about a single regional craft tradition.
The garden also has a history of collaborators, conservation and public stewardship. The foundation and institutions caring for related works provide additional perspectives.
process: SPACES Archives describes sculptures made using materials such as discarded ceramics, tiles, bangles and other recovered objects. Materials differ among the works and settings.
materials: Reused ceramic, stone and other recovered materials

sources.label: Chandigarh district: Rock Garden
SPACES Archives: Rock Garden of Chandigarh

maker.name: Nek Chand
maker.description: Nek Chand founded Chandigarh’s Rock Garden, a sculptural environment incorporating recovered materials. The John Michael Kohler Arts Center documents his work and related sculptures.

title: Delhi zardozi embroidery
region: Delhi and other Indian craft centres
intro: Metallic threads and ornament worked onto cloth.
tradition: Zardozi is practised in several regions of India, including the older quarters of Delhi. Asia InCH and Dastkari Haat Samiti document Delhi’s embroidery and the materials and workshops around it.
The term covers varied work for garments and other textiles; the maker, materials and precise techniques should be identified for each object.
process: The craft accounts describe metallic threads and decorative elements worked onto fabric, including work made using a frame and hooked needle. Materials and methods vary.

title: Kashmir papier-mâché
intro: Painted objects built on a prepared paper or wooden core.
tradition: Kashmir papier-mâché includes painted boxes, vessels and other objects. The Craft Development Institute documents the registered craft and distinguishes the body of an object from its surface painting.
An Asia InCH account distinguishes the work of sakta makers, who prepare bodies from paper pulp, from that of naqqash painters who decorate them. Some objects pass through several specialised hands.
process: The institute describes cores made from paper pulp, paperboard or light wood, followed by surface preparation and hand painting. Some pieces also use metallic decoration.
materials: Paper pulp, prepared surfaces and paint

title: Ladakhi thangka painting
region: Ladakh and the wider Himalayan region
intro: Painted scrolls made within diverse Himalayan Buddhist visual traditions.
tradition: Thangka paintings are made in Ladakh as well as other Himalayan and Tibetan Buddhist communities. Asia InCH describes painted, woven and embroidered examples, each situated in a particular religious and artistic context.
The Ladakh administration documents contemporary thangka making among several crafts. This page focuses on painting, while acknowledging that not all thangkas are painted.
process: One account describes a prepared cloth support, drawing, pigments and textile mounting. Materials and iconography depend on the maker, community and individual work.
materials: Prepared cloth, pigments and textile mounting

title: Lakshadweep coconut-shell craft
intro: Coconut shells are shaped into useful and decorative objects.
tradition: Government accounts identify coconut-shell handicrafts and coir work among the crafts of Lakshadweep. The islands have distinct communities and practices that cannot be reduced to one object.
Bowls, spoons and ornaments are among the forms documented in a NITI Aayog account. Each object has its own maker and history.
process: The government account describes polished coconut-shell objects. A shell can be shaped and smoothed for a particular use; the details differ among makers.

title: Villianur terracotta
intro: Clay sculptures and objects shaped and fired by craftspeople.
tradition: Villianur terracotta is a clay craft associated with Villianur in Puducherry. India’s geographic-indications register records the craft, and Incredible India describes a range of sculptural subjects.
The forms and purposes of individual works differ. A workshop’s story or a single object is a starting point for the craft, not a complete account.
process: The government tourism account describes shaping clay, allowing a work to dry and firing it. Coils, slabs and other construction choices depend on the piece and its maker.
